papers.what_it_is: An implementation and empirical test paper for QALS, a hybrid quantum-classical QUBO heuristic, run on a D-Wave Advantage 1.1 annealer on number partitioning and travelling salesman instances against D-Wave Hybrid, Embedding Composite, a classical exact algorithm and brute force.

existing.value: The authors state that the two implementations are in C++ and Python, run on the D-Wave machine, and are compared with the Hybrid procedure of the D-Wave suite as a baseline.
quotes: The two implementations are in C++ and Python, respectively and they run on the D-Wave machine.
As a baseline, we compared the results with the Hybrid procedure available in the D-wave suite.
existing.certainty_reason: Section 6 p.24 states the paper's own setup.

existing.note: The paper's own NPP discussion limits the conclusion: the annealer-based results come from a single (or rarely double) run because machine time was short, and the authors say QALS performance could probably improve with a much higher number of annealer measurements.
existing.value: The authors report that on the number partitioning problem the classical exact algorithm outperforms both QALS and the D-Wave Hybrid procedure, and they state that quantum annealing and QALS are not of any practical use for this problem. They also state that the annealer-based results come from a single (or rarely double) run and that QALS performance could probably improve with a much higher number of annealer measurements.

assertions.value: The authors state that the present work tests QALS on the Number Partitioning Problem (NPP) and the Travelling Salesman Problem (TSP).
quotes: The present work considers the Number Partitioning Problem (NPP) and the Travelling Salesman Problem (TSP) for the testing of QALS.
Two problems have been selected to test the performance of QALS:
assertions.certainty_reason: Abstract and Section 5 state the paper's test scope.

assertions.value: The authors define QALS as a guided meta-heuristic approach designed specifically to solve optimization problems that cannot be directly represented into the architecture of a quantum annealer.
quotes: Quantum Annealing Learning Search (QALS) is a guided meta-heuristic approach designed specifically to solve optimization problems that cannot be directly represented into the architecture of a quantum annealer.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3 opens with the paper's definition of QALS.

assertions.value: The authors describe the tabu matrix S of QALS as a sum of outer products of the solutions to be penalized, whose contribution is to penalize already visited solutions and so prevent a redundant search in the solution space. The paper attributes the approach to earlier work.
quotes: The idea of the approach suggested in [6] and further generalized in [7] is to initialize the QA by adding the so-called tabu matrix S to the weight matrix
The contribution of S is to penalize already visited solutions preventing a redundant search in the solution space.
The matrix S is constructed as the sum of outer products of the solutions to be penalized:
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited description of earlier work [6], [7]; not this paper's result.

assertions.value: The authors state that the original QALS proposal presented an argument for asymptotic convergence of the external annealing loop by reducing to a result on general tabu search, and that the original work did not include an empirical evaluation of QALS.
quotes: The authors, by reducing to a result on general tabu search, presented an argument for the asymptotic convergence of the external annealing loop (i).
However, the work did not include an empirical evaluation of QALS.
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited result of earlier work [6].
assertions.reader_inference: This paper proves no convergence result for its implementations; convergence is only inherited by citation.

assertions.value: The authors state that the tabu-based schema had not been applied to real problems on a real quantum computing architecture before this work, and that this motivates the present work.
quotes: Still, the tabu-based schema (ii) was not applied to real problems on a real quantum computing architecture, consideration that motivates the present work.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's statement of motivation and prior art.

assertions.value: The authors state that both implementations required systematic testing and some optimizations with respect to the original, mainly mathematical, formulation of QALS.
quotes: Both required systematic testing and some optimizations with respect to the original, mainly mathematical, formulation of QALS
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 4 states the implementations depart from the original formulation.

assertions.value: The authors state that, because available quantum annealer time was very short, they checked the correctness of the implementations by replacing the annealer call with an exhaustive search on the energy equation that D-Wave minimizes, and that this does not simulate a quantum annealer, which is a probabilistic machine.
quotes: the available machine time at our disposal was very short.
the call to the annealer was replaced with an exhaustive search on the same equation that D-Wave minimizes
we were not simulating the behaviour of a quantum annealer since it is a probabilistic machine.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 4 states the authors' own test setup.

assertions.value: The authors report that computing the product of the permutation matrix transpose, the QUBO matrix and the permutation matrix could take up to 100 seconds, and that a sparse representation of the permutation matrix reduced the time to about 1.5 seconds.
quotes: the time required to compute it could
take up to 100 seconds.
The execution time for this computation was reduced to ≈ 1.5 seconds, but there was still room for improvement.
assertions.certainty_reason: Started LOW: an empirical result from one study. No machine or instance size is given.

assertions.value: The authors state that permuting the matrix P has complexity O of n squared (printed O(n2)), that permuting the permutation vector perm has complexity O(n log n), and that with an inverse permutation vector the search operation becomes O(1).
quotes: The computational complexity of the permutation of P is O(n2). Instead, the permutation of perm has a complexity of O(n log n)
The resulting complexity for the search operation becomes O(1):
assertions.certainty_reason: Complexity statements without a stated proof or measurement.

assertions.value: The authors state that at the time of writing D-Wave provides only Python APIs, so a C++ program cannot directly interface with the D-Wave QPUs.
quotes: At the time of writing, D-Wave provides only Python APIs. Therefore, a C++ program can not directly interface with D-Wave’s QPUs.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's statement about a vendor interface at one date.

assertions.value: The authors state that the C++ implementation, because the Leap IDE does not provide the Python.h header, starts a Python child process by a fork operation and exchanges the topology, the problem entries and the solution with it through anonymous pipes.
quotes: the QALS algorithm is run on the Leap IDE, which does not provide the required Python.h header.
In the second approach (the one that has been used), at the startup, the C++ executable generates a Python child process by means of a fork operation.
the Python process ﬁrst retrieves the annealer’s topology and sends it to the C++ process via an anonymous pipe.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 4.1 describes the paper's own implementation design.

assertions.value: The authors report that the message exchange between the C++ process and the Python process took about 1 second with 5000 variables, measured without calling the quantum annealer, and they state that this might cancel the benefit of using C++ instead of Python.
quotes: The transmission took ≈ 1 second using 5000 variables, which is almost the Pegasus architecture limit.
it might cancel the beneﬁt of using C ++ instead of Python.
assertions.certainty_reason: Started LOW: an empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that the modulo operation on C++ rand() does not give numbers with equal probability, that the period of rand() is typically the value printed as 232 (an exponent printed flat, two to the power thirty-two) but depends on the implementation, and that rand() was therefore not a reasonable choice for permuting vectors with more than 5000 variables.
quotes: the modulo operation (used to restrict the generated numbers to the required range) does not yield numbers with equal probability.
The period of rand() is typically 232, but it depends on the implementations.
Since the algorithm presented in [6] has to permute vectors with more than 5000 variables, rand() was not a reasonable choice.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's argument with a textbook modulo-bias example; no measurement.

assertions.value: The authors report that generating random numbers with the quantum annealer would need 13 runs of about 0.3 seconds each, about 3.9 seconds of overhead per QALS iteration, and they state that it is not a feasible approach.
quotes: each run of Algorithm 7 requires around 0.3 seconds (on average).
the overhead for each iteration of QALS would be around 3.9 seconds.
the quantum annealer would be called 13 times more than usual
Obviously, it is not a feasible approach.
assertions.certainty_reason: Started LOW: an empirical result from one study. An estimate from the stated figures.

assertions.value: The authors state that they chose the Mersenne Twister, with a period printed as 219937 − 1 (an exponent printed flat, two to the power nineteen thousand nine hundred thirty-seven, minus one), for the C++ random numbers.
quotes: In the end, we chose the Mersenne Twister, which uses a period of 219937 − 1.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 4.1 states the paper's own implementation choice.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Mersenne Twister does not guarantee quality in random number generation and is not sufficient to produce all possible sequences, and call it the best compromise they found between efficiency and coverage of the space of permutations.

Although it is not suﬃcient to produce all possible sequences, it is the best compromise we found between eﬃciency and coverage of the space of permutations.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 4.1 states the limit of the authors' own generator choice.

assertions.value: The authors state that the NPP QUBO formulation used, taken from a tutorial, minimises the squared difference of the two subset sums and gives the matrix entries Qii = si (si − c) and Qij = Qji = sisj, where c is the sum of the numbers.
quotes: experiments has been taken from [20].
Qii = si (si − c) Qij = Qji = sisj
Instead of directly minimizing the diﬀerence, let us minimize its value squared
assertions.certainty_reason: A formulation cited from Glover et al. [20].

quotes: The solution to the QUBO problem is x = (1,1,1,1,0,0,1,0), for which y = -2704
assertions.certainty_reason: An arithmetic illustration; not an experiment.
assertions.reader_inference: The listed x selects 8, 21, 6, 7 and 10 (index 7, 1-based), summing to 52 of the total 104, which matches a zero difference.

assertions.value: The authors state that the number partitioning problem can be considered practically solved by the available classical exact solution.
quotes: the problem can be considered practically solved by the available classical exact solution.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's judgment.

assertions.value: The authors state that the C++ implementation has better performance in the classical part but pays the price of coupling with the D-Wave APIs, which are available in Python only, and that for this reason the Python implementation proves to be competitive.
quotes: The implementation in C++ has the advantage of having better performance in the classical part
for this very reason, the Python implementation proves to be competitive.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim; no head-to-head timing of the two implementations is reported in the text.

assertions.value: The authors argue that the availability of C++ interfaces to the D-Wave machines, once present and now apparently discontinued, would make the development of efficient hybrid algorithms easier.
quotes: We argue that the availability of C++ interfaces to the D-Wave machines, once present and now apparently discontinued, would make the development of eﬃcient hybrid algorithms easier.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's argument.

assertions.value: The authors state that the comparison with Hybrid is a necessary baseline but, because Hybrid is a race among different algorithms, it cannot be an effective competitor for drawing scientific conclusions.
quotes: We note that the comparison with respect to Hybrid is a necessary baseline but, given its nature of race among diﬀerent algorithms, cannot be an eﬀective competitor for drawing scientiﬁc conclusions.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 6 states a limit on what the Hybrid comparison supports.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that their implementations of QALS work on TSP and could have practical potential on hard problems where the QUBO representation is not directly mappable to the topology.
quotes: We conclude that our implementations of QALS work on TSP and could have practical potential on hard problems where the QUBO representation is not directly mappable to the topology.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's conclusion, hedged with 'could'.

assertions.value: The authors state that the large qubit counts of commercial annealers led to the expectation that annealers could in principle, for specific problems, provide solutions that outperform classical counterparts.
quotes: This led to the expectation that the application of quantum annealers could in principle, for speciﬁc problems, provide solutions that outperform classical counterparts
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's statement of background expectation.
